items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we have two vectors [MATH: \textbf{u}=\langle 1, 3 \rangle] and [MATH: \textbf{v}=\langle 2,-1 \rangle.] The parallelogram spanned by [MATH: \textbf{u}] and [MATH: \textbf{v}] is shown in the picture below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b71bd81a49f801c9f5e115e8d2f89fb9]

Content:
Now, we construct a new matrix

Content:
[MATH: [1|2; 3|− 1]]

Content:
where the columns are made up of the components of the corresponding vectors. Let's find the determinant of [MATH: M\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: det(M)|=|1|2; 3|− 1|; = 1 ⋅ (− 1) − 2 ⋅ 3; = − 7]

Content:
It turns out that the absolute value of [MATH: \det(M)] gives the area [MATH: A] of the parallelogram:

Content:
[MATH: A|=|det(M)|; =|− 7|; = 7]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we construct a matrix where the columns are made up of the components of the corresponding vectors:

[MATH: [1|3; 2|− 3]]

Then, we find the determinant:

[MATH: det(M)|=|1|3; 2|− 3|; = 1 ⋅ (− 3) − 3 ⋅ 2; = − 9]

The absolute value of [MATH: \det(M)] gives the area [MATH: A] of the parallelogram:

[MATH: A = |{-9}| = 9]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Why does the absolute value of the determinant represent the area of the parallelogram? Let's prove this result.

Content:
First, let's state the result precisely. Consider two vectors [MATH: \textbf{u}=\langle a,b \rangle] and [MATH: \textbf{v}=\langle c,d \rangle.] The parallelogram spanned by [MATH: \textbf{u}] and [MATH: \textbf{v}] is shown in the picture below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/98f405fbc70b5a40be2c5ce94bda673f]

Content:
We construct a new matrix

Content:
[MATH: [a|c; b|d]]

Content:
where the columns are made up of the components of the corresponding vectors. Then the absolute value of [MATH: \det(M)] gives the area [MATH: A] of the parallelogram spanned by [MATH: \textbf{u}] and [MATH: \textbf{v}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: A = |\det(M)|]

Content:
To prove the formula, we use the following picture:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9a2676dd42afc9d49fc56932dbcac477]

Content:
We can compute the area by starting with the area of the outer rectangle, and then subtracting off the area of the smaller triangles and rectangles surrounding the parallelogram:

Content:
[MATH: A|=|(a + c)(b + d) − 2 ⋅ (1)/(2)cd− 2 ⋅ ad− 2 ⋅ (1)/(2)ab|; =|ab + ad + bc + cd − cd − 2ad − ab|; =|bc − ad|; =|ad − bc|; =|det(M)|]

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Case When Two Vectors are Parallel

Content:
When two vectors are parallel, the parallelogram does not exist. So, it has zero area.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/378bd116b22c5d0b45b09152520e42c0]

Content:
As a result, the determinant of a matrix whose columns are parallel vectors must also be zero.

Content:
For example, in the diagram above, we have the vectors [MATH: \textbf{u} = \left< 1,1 \right>] and [MATH: \textbf{v} = \left< 2,2 \right>.] Constructing a matrix where the columns are made up of the components of the corresponding vectors, we have

Content:
[MATH: [1|2; 1|2]]

Content:
Indeed, the determinant does come out to zero:

Content:
[MATH: det(M)|=|1|2; 1|2|; = 1 ⋅ 2 − 2 ⋅ 1; = 0]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we construct a matrix where the columns are made up of the components of the corresponding vectors:

[MATH: [3|6; − 2|− 4]]

Then, we find the determinant:

[MATH: det(M)|=|3|6; − 2|− 4|; = 3 ⋅ (− 4) − 6 ⋅ (− 2); = 0]

The absolute value of [MATH: \det(M)] gives the area [MATH: A] of the parallelogram:

[MATH: A = |\,0\,| = 0]

Item 9 — Tutorial: General Rule

Content:
Why does the absolute value of the determinant represent the area of the parallelogram? Let's prove this result.

Content:
First, let's state the result precisely. Consider two vectors [MATH: \textbf{u}=\langle a,b \rangle] and [MATH: \textbf{v}=\langle c,d \rangle.] The parallelogram spanned by [MATH: \textbf{u}] and [MATH: \textbf{v}] is shown in the picture below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/98f405fbc70b5a40be2c5ce94bda673f]

Content:
We construct a new matrix

Content:
[MATH: [a|c; b|d]]

Content:
where the columns are made up of the components of the corresponding vectors. Then the absolute value of [MATH: \det(M)] gives the area [MATH: A] of the parallelogram spanned by [MATH: \textbf{u}] and [MATH: \textbf{v}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: A = |\det(M)|]

Content:
To prove the formula, we use the following picture:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9a2676dd42afc9d49fc56932dbcac477]

Content:
We can compute the area by starting with the area of the outer rectangle, and then subtracting off the area of the smaller triangles and rectangles surrounding the parallelogram:

Content:
[MATH: A|=|(a + c)(b + d) − 2 ⋅ (1)/(2)cd− 2 ⋅ ad− 2 ⋅ (1)/(2)ab|; =|ab + ad + bc + cd − cd − 2ad − ab|; =|bc − ad|; =|ad − bc|; =|det(M)|]
